questions.prompt: Why is it risky to rely entirely on color to communicate an error?

options.text: Individuals with color vision deficiencies may not perceive the difference between the colors.
Color cannot be rendered correctly on mobile devices.
Red and green are universally considered positive colors.
Automated tools cannot measure the color red.

questions.explanation: If a hue is the only indicator, someone who cannot perceive that specific hue may miss the information.
questions.hint: Think about how someone with red-green color blindness experiences an interface.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Understand why color alone is insufficient for conveying information.

questions.prompt: How does lightness contrast assist users with color vision deficiencies?

options.text: It automatically shifts colors to a grayscale palette.
It provides a secondary visual cue that does not depend on hue perception.
It increases the physical size of the text elements.
It triggers an audio description of the color being used.

questions.explanation: Even if two hues look similar, a difference in lightness can keep them visibly distinct.
questions.hint: Focus on the difference between light and dark rather than red and blue.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Identify how lightness contrast creates a secondary visual cue.

questions.prompt: Which is a safe way to indicate a text link?

options.text: Making the link text slightly lighter than the body text.
Using only a bright blue color for the link.
Pairing a distinct color with a solid underline.
Removing the border from the element entirely.

questions.explanation: An underline adds a shape-based indicator, so the link can be recognized without relying only on color.
questions.hint: A robust design pairs color with an additional physical indicator.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Combine color with other design elements to ensure clarity.
